words.definition: a short plan of the main points
words.example: Before writing, make an {outline} of your three main arguments.

words.definition: to name a book or writer as support for what you say
words.example: In your essay, {cite} two experts by name to support your main argument.

words.definition: to say the same thing using different words
words.example: Try to {paraphrase} the text: keep its meaning but put it in your own words.

words.definition: copying someone else's work and saying it is yours
words.example: Copying a whole essay from a website is {plagiarism}.

words.definition: a list of the books and other sources you used
words.example: List every book and website you used in the {bibliography} at the end of your project.

words.definition: suitable for serious or official situations
words.example: Don't use slang in a {formal} letter to the head teacher.

words.definition: clear and logical, with parts that fit together well
words.example: Her essay was {coherent}: each paragraph followed logically from the one before.

words.definition: to give more details or explain an idea more fully
words.example: Your point is interesting, but please {elaborate}: give us some examples.

words.definition: the number of words in a text
words.example: Check the {word count}; the limit is three hundred.

words.definition: to say the opposite of what someone else has said
words.example: The two witnesses {contradict} each other: one says the car was red, the other says blue.

words.definition: to think that something is true without checking
words.example: Don't {assume} that everyone in the class has a smartphone.

words.definition: to be greater or more important than something else
words.example: The benefits of exercise far {outweigh} the risks of getting a small injury.

words.definition: based on good reasons and facts
words.example: Your reason for missing the test is {valid}: being ill is a good excuse.

words.definition: a reason given against another argument
words.example: A good essay answers each {counter-argument} fairly.

words.definition: causing a lot of strong disagreement
words.example: Testing on animals is {controversial}: some people strongly support it and others strongly oppose it.

words.definition: a particular way of thinking about something
words.example: Try to see the problem from your parents' {perspective}.

words.definition: to accept or admit that something is true
words.example: She knew she was wrong but refused to {acknowledge} her mistake in public.

words.definition: certainly true; impossible to doubt
words.example: With so much clear evidence, it is {undeniable} that the planet is getting warmer.

words.definition: a statement that says something is true of every case
words.example: 'All teenagers are lazy' is a {generalisation}: it says something is true of every teenager.

words.definition: an idea that has not yet been proved and needs to be tested
words.example: Before the experiment, write down your {hypothesis}: what you predict will happen.

words.definition: the information that people discover from research
words.example: The survey's {findings} showed that most students sleep less than eight hours.

words.definition: to decide what something means
words.example: How do you {interpret} this graph? I think it shows prices are rising.

words.definition: a set of ideas that explains why something happens
words.example: Darwin's {theory} of evolution changed biology for ever.

words.definition: people in an experiment who do not get the treatment being tested, so they can be compared with the others
words.example: Half the patients got the new drug, and the {control group} got sugar pills.

words.definition: a set of questions you ask many people to find out what they think
words.example: We did a {survey} of two hundred students to find out how they get to school.

words.definition: not giving a clear answer or result
words.example: The data neither proved nor disproved our idea, so the results were {inconclusive}.

words.definition: an important new discovery
words.example: After years of failed experiments, the scientists made a {breakthrough} and found a cure.

words.definition: large or important enough to be noticed
words.example: The change was not tiny; it was {significant} enough for everyone to notice.

words.definition: to try to find out the truth about something
words.example: Detectives are trying to {investigate} the burglary.

words.definition: protection that a country gives to someone who has escaped danger in their own country
words.example: Fleeing the war, the family asked for {asylum}: permission to stay safely in a new country.

words.definition: treating people unfairly because of who they are
words.example: Laws protect workers from {discrimination} because of their age.

words.definition: the state of being very poor
words.example: Millions of children around the world live in {poverty}.

words.definition: having no place to live
words.example: The charity gives hot meals to {homeless} people.

words.definition: the smaller part of a group; less than half
words.example: Only a small {minority} of students, three out of thirty, voted against the plan.

words.definition: a charity that hands out free tins and packets to people who cannot afford to eat
words.example: Our school collects tins every December for the local {food bank}.

words.definition: money the government pays to people who are ill, poor or out of work
words.example: Because she is too ill to work, she gets {benefits}, money paid by the government.

words.definition: a person who has come to live in a new country
words.example: As an {immigrant} from Portugal, my grandfather had to learn English when he moved here.

words.definition: the basic freedoms that every person should have
words.example: Free speech is one of our most important {human rights}.

words.definition: a written list of what a political party promises to do if it wins
words.example: Before the election, the party's {manifesto} listed fifty promises, from free buses to lower taxes.

words.definition: the group of people elected to make a country's laws
words.example: The new law was passed by {parliament} last week.

words.definition: a document signed by many people asking someone in power to do something
words.example: Over five thousand people signed our {petition} asking the council to keep the library open.

words.definition: the political parties that are not in the government
words.example: The leader of the {opposition} attacked the government's plan and promised to scrap it if her party won.

words.definition: a country whose head of state is not a king or queen
words.example: In a {republic}, the head of state is usually elected instead of inheriting the role from a parent.

words.definition: a system in which a king or queen is the head of a country
words.example: In a {monarchy}, the role of head of state usually passes to another member of the royal family.

words.definition: a public show that people strongly disagree with something
words.example: Thousands marched through the streets in a peaceful {protest}.

words.definition: a senior member of a government
words.example: The health {minister} opened the new hospital.

words.definition: money that people must pay to the government
words.example: Part of what you earn goes to the government as {tax}.

words.definition: a secret vote, or the paper on which you vote
words.example: In the school election, each pupil marked one name on the {ballot} and put it in a box.

words.definition: the system of money, trade and jobs in a country
words.example: Tourism is very important to the {economy} of Greece.

words.definition: a general rise in prices
words.example: Because of {inflation}, prices across the whole economy rose, so our weekly shopping cost five per cent more.

words.definition: a situation when there is not enough of something
words.example: Because of the dry summer, there is a {shortage} of water and we can't fill the pool.

words.definition: how much money people need to pay for basic things like rent and food
words.example: London's {cost of living} is high because rent and food cost more there than elsewhere in the UK.

words.definition: to help something increase or improve
words.example: Lower prices could {boost} sales and bring more customers into the shops.

words.definition: a person who buys goods or services
words.example: A careful {consumer} compares prices in several shops before buying anything.

words.definition: to sell goods to another country
words.example: Countries like Brazil {export} coffee all over the world.

words.definition: to buy goods from another country
words.example: Britain has to {import} almost all of its bananas.

words.definition: a time when a country's trade and business fall
words.example: Many people lost their jobs during the {recession}.

words.definition: an increase in the money you get for your work
words.example: After a great year, my mum's boss gave her a {pay rise} of five per cent.

words.definition: to leave your job because you choose to
words.example: He decided to {resign} from his job and travel the world.

words.definition: to discuss something in order to reach an agreement
words.example: The union will {negotiate} a better pay deal with the bosses.

words.definition: a document listing your education and jobs, sent with a job application
words.example: Attach your {CV}, which lists your education and past jobs, to every job application.

words.definition: a short period of work that gives a student experience
words.example: She did a summer {internship} at a law firm.

words.definition: the amount of work you have to do
words.example: My {workload} is so heavy that I am at my desk until nine.

words.definition: doing or achieving a lot
words.example: I'm most {productive} in the morning: I get more work done before lunch than after.

words.definition: working well together in a group
words.example: Our {teamwork} was excellent: everyone in the group shared the jobs and helped each other.

words.definition: to travel regularly between home and work
words.example: Many people {commute} to London by train every day.

words.definition: a person who starts their own business
words.example: Anyone who starts their own business is an {entrepreneur}, like my aunt with her bakery.

words.definition: a short phrase that is easy to remember, used in advertising
words.example: The company's {slogan}, 'Fresh every day', is printed on every bag.

words.definition: the group of people a product or message is meant for
words.example: Teenagers are the {target audience} for this new game.

words.definition: a person with many online followers who can affect what those followers buy
words.example: The {influencer} was paid to show the face cream to her two million followers.

words.definition: a company that pays for an event or team in return for advertising
words.example: A bank is the football club's main {sponsor}: it pays to have its name on every shirt.

words.definition: stopping people from seeing, reading or hearing certain things
words.example: Under strict {censorship}, newspapers could not criticise the king.

words.definition: a short video showing parts of a new film to advertise it
words.example: We watched the {trailer} for the new film, and now I can't wait to see it.

words.definition: easy to remember, especially a song or a slogan
words.example: The advert had such a {catchy} tune that I sang it all day.

words.definition: a headline or picture that makes you click a link, often to something disappointing
words.example: That shocking headline was just {clickbait}: the article itself was boring and had nothing new.

words.definition: to pay regularly to receive something
words.example: I {subscribe} to a science magazine that comes every month.

words.definition: a person whose job is to give opinions about books, films, plays or art
words.example: The newspaper's {critic} gave the new film only one star out of five.

words.definition: singing, acting or playing music in front of an audience
words.example: After weeks of rehearsals, her first {performance} as Juliet in front of an audience was brilliant.

words.definition: a film or book that continues the story of an earlier one
words.example: The first film was so popular that they made a {sequel} two years later.

words.definition: a room or building where works of art are shown
words.example: The paintings hang in a {gallery} with white walls and high windows.

words.definition: a person who writes plays
words.example: Shakespeare is England's most famous {playwright}.

words.definition: a large painting on a wall
words.example: Students covered the playground wall with a huge {mural} of trees, birds and flowers.

words.definition: the first public showing of a film or play
words.example: The actors walked down the red carpet at the film's {premiere} in London.

words.definition: a large group of musicians who play different instruments together
words.example: The {orchestra} has over eighty musicians, from violins to drums.

words.definition: all the actors in a film or play
words.example: The play has a {cast} of twelve actors, but only four of them have big parts.

words.definition: able to break down naturally without harming the environment
words.example: These cups are {biodegradable}, so they rot away in a few months instead of lasting for years.

words.definition: the variety of plants and animals in a place
words.example: Scientists counted every kind of plant and animal in the forest to measure its {biodiversity}.

words.definition: cutting down large areas of forest
words.example: Farming for palm oil has led to {deforestation} in Borneo.

words.definition: the amount of carbon dioxide that your activities produce
words.example: Flying less is one way to shrink your {carbon footprint}.

words.definition: protecting nature and wildlife
words.example: The charity works on the {conservation} of rare birds.

words.definition: the rise in the temperature of the Earth's air and oceans
words.example: Melting ice at the poles is a sign of {global warming}.

words.definition: grown without artificial chemicals
words.example: These {organic} carrots were grown without any artificial chemicals.

words.definition: a place where rubbish is buried under the ground
words.example: Most plastic ends up in {landfill} or in the sea.

words.definition: a flat object that turns sunlight into electricity
words.example: We put a {solar panel} on the roof of the shed.

words.definition: a feeling of worry and nervousness
words.example: Before exams, many students feel {anxiety}: a racing heart, sweaty hands and constant worry.

words.definition: to deal successfully with something difficult
words.example: How do you {cope} with the pressure of exams?

words.definition: the wish to do something
words.example: I've lost all my {motivation} to practise the piano.

words.definition: the health of your mind and feelings
words.example: Look after your {mental health} as carefully as you look after your body.

words.definition: able to recover quickly from difficulties
words.example: Children are often {resilient}: after a bad day, they bounce back very quickly.

words.definition: how much you like and value yourself
words.example: Children with low {self-esteem} often believe they are worse than everyone else.

words.definition: feeling that there is too much to deal with
words.example: With five exams in a week, I felt completely {overwhelmed}.

words.definition: a problem with getting to sleep or staying asleep
words.example: Lying awake night after night, unable to fall asleep, is called {insomnia}.

words.definition: treatment that helps someone with problems of the mind or body
words.example: After the accident, she had {therapy} to help her walk again.

words.definition: computer systems that can learn and make decisions
words.example: Self-driving cars use {artificial intelligence} to learn from experience and make decisions on the road.

words.definition: a set of steps that a computer follows to solve a problem
words.example: Write an {algorithm}: a list of steps the computer must follow to sort these numbers.

words.definition: using machines to do work that people used to do
words.example: Factory {automation} has replaced many workers.

words.definition: a new idea or a new way of doing something
words.example: The company rewards {innovation}: staff who come up with new ideas get a bonus.

words.definition: a computer world that seems real when you wear a headset
words.example: With {virtual reality}, you can walk around ancient Rome.

words.definition: to change information into a secret code
words.example: Secure apps {encrypt} your messages so that nobody else can read them.

words.definition: to get into a computer system without permission
words.example: Someone tried to {hack} into the school's computers.

words.definition: no longer used because something newer exists
words.example: Video tapes became {obsolete} when DVDs arrived.

words.definition: the newest and most advanced
words.example: The hospital has the newest, most advanced scanners: truly {cutting-edge} equipment.

words.definition: to try hard
words.example: You should {make an effort} to talk to the new student.

words.definition: to get better at something or move forward
words.example: After months of hard practice, she is finally starting to {make progress} with her Spanish.

words.definition: to accept that something is your duty or your fault
words.example: Leaders must {take responsibility} for their decisions.

words.definition: to make good use of a chance
words.example: You should {take advantage of} the sunny weather and go outside.

words.definition: to harm something
words.example: Strong winds can {do damage} to old buildings.

words.definition: to be easy to understand
words.example: I've read this instruction three times, but it still doesn't {make sense} to me.

words.definition: to think about something when you decide or judge
words.example: The judges will {take into account} the age of each dancer.

words.definition: to earn the money you need to live
words.example: Few musicians earn enough money to {make a living} from their music alone.

words.definition: to watch, listen or think carefully
words.example: Please {pay attention} while I explain the safety rules.

words.definition: to do a task or a piece of work
words.example: Scientists {carry out} tests on new medicines.

words.definition: to make someone notice a fact
words.example: She was kind enough to {point out} my spelling mistake so that I could fix it.

words.definition: to look after a child until it is an adult
words.example: My grandparents helped to {bring up} my brother and me.

words.definition: to stop working, of a machine or vehicle
words.example: Our old car tends to {break down} on long journeys.

words.definition: to do or use less of something
words.example: I'm trying to {cut down on} sugar.

words.definition: to understand or solve something after thinking
words.example: I can't {figure out} how to open this box.

words.definition: to be very easy to notice
words.example: Her bright red coat made her {stand out} in the crowd.

words.definition: to happen or end in a particular way, often a surprising one
words.example: We planned a quiet party, but it didn't {turn out} that way: forty people came.

words.definition: to need someone or something and trust them to help
words.example: You can always {rely on} me to help with your homework.

words.definition: connected with trade, industry and money
words.example: The country is going through an {economic} crisis.

words.definition: using little money, fuel or time
words.example: This small car is {economical}: it uses very little petrol, so it's cheap to run.

words.definition: easily upset by what people say or do
words.example: He's very {sensitive} about his height, so don't tease him.

words.definition: so important that people will remember it for a long time
words.example: Today's vote is {historic}: people will still be talking about it in a hundred years.

words.definition: connected with the past
words.example: She loves reading {historical} novels set in Tudor times.

words.definition: a basic rule or belief that guides what you do
words.example: I never eat meat; it's a matter of {principle}.

words.definition: to put something down carefully
words.example: Please {lay} the baby gently in the cot.

words.definition: to be in a flat position on a bed or the ground
words.example: I need to {lie} down for a while; I feel dizzy.

words.definition: to leave your own country to live in another one
words.example: Her family decided to {emigrate} to Canada.

words.definition: all the subjects that are taught in a school
words.example: The {curriculum} lists all the subjects a school teaches, from maths to music.

words.definition: that must be done because of a rule or law
words.example: At our school, wearing a uniform is {compulsory}; nobody may come in jeans.

words.definition: a test or judgement of how well someone is doing
words.example: The final {assessment} for the course is a spoken presentation.

words.definition: the ability to read and write
words.example: In our town, adults with poor {literacy} can join free classes to learn to read and write.

words.definition: teaching the skills needed for a particular job
words.example: She chose a {vocational} course in hairdressing.

words.definition: staying away from school without permission
words.example: The school is worried about {truancy}, as some pupils skip lessons without permission.

words.definition: to make a pupil leave a school for ever as a punishment
words.example: The head teacher decided to {expel} him, so he can never come back to the school.

words.definition: a school where pupils live during the term
words.example: At {boarding school}, she only saw her family in the holidays.

words.definition: done in addition to normal lessons
words.example: After lessons end, the school offers chess, drama and other {extracurricular} activities.
